bearings.paper_claim: Donor label raised senior access in 191 House offices of one party, June to August 2013: chief of staff or above 12.5% vs 2.4% (p=.006), legislative director or above 18.8% vs 5.5% (p=.005), Member 7.8% vs 2.4% (p=.07). Ratios implied by Table 1: about 5.2, 3.4 and 3.2. The paper reports no effect on votes or positions.
bearings.paper_location: Table 1 p.552; text p.553-554; fn 11 p.553; influence limitation p.555
bearings.system_side: pflip(n) = a/(a+b) at flip_model.py:92-96 puts a saturating CU-money term with WM 0.35 directly into a member's flip probability, against a peer term with WP 0.65. The CALIBRATED comment at flip_model.py:21 lists Kalla and Broockman among sources for money buys access/effort greater than votes.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports only the access step: one 2013 experiment, one liberal group, one bill, one party's House offices, a randomized donor label rather than dollars. It gives no estimate of WM, WP, HALFF or saturation, and no effect on votes or positions (p.555). The citation supports access before votes only if narrowed to access; the not-votes half is outside the paper.
bearings.verifier_note: All Table 1 numbers reproduced. Ratios 5.2, 3.4 and 3.2 are arithmetic from Table 1; the abstract says three to four times. Line 21 cites the paper for the greater-than-votes half, which the paper does not address, so the cite must be narrowed to access. The paper calibrates no constant.

bearings.paper_claim: The seniority of the official who attends responded to a randomized donor label across 191 offices over about three months. Cosponsorship as an outcome tells us little: nine legislators cosponsored in total, with the same share in both arms, and the authors say the estimate is too uncertain to bear on access effects.
bearings.paper_location: Table 1 p.552; outcome coding p.552; fn 11 p.553
bearings.system_side: H1 correlates frozen seed_prob with new cosponsorship count deltas by Spearman rank, requiring at least 60 days and at least 150 members with any delta. These thresholds match PROTOCOL_TEXT at outcome_contract.py:17-20. The summary's F5 replay figure of 72 of 511 new-event members was not found in the engine code or docs searched.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The transfer concerns outcome choice, not effect size. A seniority-of-attendee outcome needs a real outreach log, which the system does not have, plus its own pre-registered single look. Any result stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062). Do not use the 72 of 511 figure until it is located.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper claims reproduced from the text. The 72 of 511 figure could not be located in the repo, so it is removed as unsupported. Cosponsorship was described as telling us little, not as uninformative.

bearings.paper_claim: Who is asked changes which tier takes the meeting. The donor label raised chief-of-staff-or-above access (12.5% vs 2.4%, p=.006) but not access at the district-staff tier (48.4% vs 43.3%, p=.26).
bearings.paper_location: Table 1 p.552; design pp.550-552; fn 7 p.550
bearings.system_side: The router returns the least-cost introduction route to staff anchored at a member office. A member-context modifier of 1 + MEMBER_BETA times value is applied to terminal costs (staffer_closeness_routes.py:913-918 and 1014). MEMBER_BETA = 0.15 is defined at closeness_math.py:21. Route costs are heuristic outputs, not access probabilities (D-025).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports recording the seniority of the person reached as a validation target, matching its six-rank coding. It does not justify converting route costs or ranks into access probabilities, which would break D-025. The paper measured a requester attribute in district-office meetings, not a warm introduction through a co-worker tie.
bearings.verifier_note: Numbers reproduced. The claim that MEMBER_BETA is explicitly not access evidence is not in the code at the cited lines or in closeness_math.py, so it is removed. The code citation is corrected to closeness_math.py:21.

bearings.paper_claim: When an organized group tells an office its members are local campaign donors, senior officials attend more often than when described as constituents: three to four times in the abstract; Table 1 ratios about 3.2 for Member, 3.4 for legislative director or above, and 5.2 for chief of staff or above.
bearings.paper_location: Abstract p.545; Table 1 p.552; limitations p.555
bearings.system_side: Sphere of Influence = 0.45 giving + 0.45 volunteering + 0.10 household. Giving G = (charitable + cpi_donor)/4 + contrib_high/2. The weights status is a leaning ruling (framework_config.json:2556-2557).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper bears only on donor status made known to an office through an organized group's request. It says nothing about charitable giving, volunteering, or individuals acting alone, and it covers one liberal organization in 2013. Use it to justify revealing donor status in organized asks, not to reweight the giving term. The config does not define contrib_high, so its mapping to donor status is unverified.
bearings.verifier_note: Formula and leaning status reproduced. The 3 to 5 times wording does not match the paper, which says three and four times in the abstract; the ratios are given instead. The paper gives no basis for the volunteering or household weights.

bearings.paper_claim: Offices were blocked on Obama's 2012 two-party vote share among six covariates, with omnibus balance p=.92 (chi-square 1.44, 5 df). The paper reports no heterogeneity of the donor-label effect by seat competitiveness.
bearings.paper_location: Blocking and balance pp.549-550 (balance result p.549)
bearings.system_side: c = 1 + AMPLITUDE*exp(-max(lean,0)/SCALE) multiplies effective dollars on both money legs. AMPLITUDE = 1.0 and SCALE = 5.0 are judgment constants, labeled uncalibrated, and the reciprocity they encode is not validated.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Blocking on partisanship balances it across arms but does not estimate whether the donor effect differs in competitive seats; 64 treated offices could not have estimated that. The paper gives no support for c. The multiplier stays unvalidated (D-104..D-108).
bearings.verifier_note: Balance p=.92 and chi-square 1.44 with 5 df are on p.549, not p.550. The constants and the uncalibrated label verified at moneyball_core.py:83 and 90-93.

bearings.paper_claim: The measured outcome was access: the rank of the official who attended. Positions and votes were not measured. Cosponsorship was nine legislators in total, with equal shares in both arms, and the authors say it tells little about effects.
bearings.paper_location: Outcome p.552; fn 11 p.553; influence limitation p.555
bearings.system_side: MAXSHIFT = 18, labeled CALIBRATED from 40 on the premise that money moves positions little and buys access and effort, not votes (money_response.py:15-17). LOSSFRAME = 1.10 treats competitor spending as a loss frame (money_response.py:31). The code cites Ansolabehere and Fowler-Garro-Spenkuch for this premise, not this paper.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper can be cited for the access measure, but not for a null on positions: its cosponsorship estimate is uninformative rather than null. It says nothing about MAXSHIFT, HALF, DTHRESH or LOSSFRAME. The not-votes half of the premise lies outside the paper (p.555).
bearings.verifier_note: The paper claim matches the text. The code premise is cited to other sources, so this paper cannot be added as support for the not-votes part. Lines 15 and 31 verified.

related.why: Survey experiment on 441 DC congressional staffers about money and information. Together with this field experiment it bears on the mechanism question the authors leave open.
Kim, Stuckatz and Wolters test whether donations precede lobbying on bills in observational LDA and FEC data. This randomized donor label supports the access step those sequences assume.
Furnas, LaPira and Brock show low overlap between organizational lobbying and PAC spending, which limits how often a donor label is available to lobbying actors.
Blackwell and Yamauchi address unmeasured confounding in observational political-ad effects after Citizens United, the confounding problem this randomized design avoids.

Bonica and Grumbach show campaign money is much older than the electorate and wealth is concentrated. Their text also cites this paper's donor-access result. Relevant to who can credibly present as a donor.
Holyoke, Brown and LaPira describe lobbyist relationships built on mutual need. This experiment shows the donor signal shifts which staff tier engages.
